analytic.title: Guaranteeing End-to-end Deadlines in Distributed Client-Server Applications

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper presents a scheme for guaranteeing the scheduling of real-time computations in a distributed environment. We propose a process model where only true local or end-to-end deadlines need t o b e s p eci ed. We assume all local interactions among processes are based on shared memory communication, protected by priority ceiling semaphores. Remote interactions are clientserver blocking communications. The result is both a scheduling policy and a methodology to guarantee the integrated scheduling of processes and network messages. Both processes and messages are scheduled a c cording to a xed-priority scheme that can easily be implemented on most operating systems and a few network protocols. The procedure that checks the schedulability of the distributed computation against end-to-end deadlines is simple enough to be p r oposed as a scheme for a dynamic guarantee

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time scheduling theory has produced remarkable results for the single processor case. Most of the application designers, on the other hand, must face the problem of how to design distributed real-time applications where the timing constraints do not apply to the individual tasks but to the end-to-end computations. The distributed scheduling problem is less understood and the research community is proposing a few approaches that answer some of the basic questions usually restricting the model of the system. The problem of scheduling real-time tasks in a distributed environment i s t wofold: we m ust specify the timing constraints of the application and derive a process model where the timing constraints apply to processes and tasks, and we must solve the process scheduling problem. The latter is of exponential di culty in the general case e.g. integrated scheduling of tasks and messages with end-to-end deadlines and any t ype of precedence constraints, local and remote resource sharing and for most practical purposes. The problem of mapping application constraints often endto-end deadlines into process and message deadlines is an open problem. A solutions has been proposed in 3 for a single processor subcase. In the general case distributed computations, deadline partitioning is often done by hand, or by some reasonable heuristic, almost never on the basis of the actual load of the local nodes.

Our solution automatically assigns the intermediate deadlines to the messages and the remote tasks. These are computed as functions of the end-to-end deadlines and the computation time of the component tasks network transmission time for the messages, but also of the load of the nodes where they run. This paper tries to give a solution to an instance of the real-time scheduling problem which allows for a broad range of architectural choices, accounts for end-to-end deadlines and consists of the integrated scheduling and guarantee of both tasks and messages. Our study is made possible by the choice of a restricted, although hopefully common, programming style, which limits the type of remote interaction to a collection of nested client-server interactions with a blocking semantics. Client and server processes can locally share resources, using the well known priority ceiling and stack resource policies 2 1 . The guarantee formula is simple enough to be used by a dynamic scheduling policy that dynamically accepts remote computations by recomputing the schedulability conditions at all nodes.

Our solution is similar to 7 where a procedure called holistic scheduling is used to schedule periodic transactions in a distributed environment. The main di erences with the previous approach are: rst, the paper on holistic scheduling gives an extremely elegant formula for checking the schedulability, but assumes that tasks and messages have user de ned priorities and it is not clear how these priorities can be extracted from the end-toend deadlines. The second di erence is in the type of analysis that is performed. The cited paper contains an iterative analysis for checking the schedulability conditions. The non periodicity of the remote invocations of tasks and messages is modeled using a jitter parameter which is included in the schedulability analysis. Our schedulability analysis is in the form of closed formulas which hopefully makes the method a possible choice for a dynamic system and the non periodicity of remote tasks and messages is modeled by making worst case assumptions. On the other hand, our formula is clearly pessimistic and only deals with a subset of all possible task con gurations. Other distributed scheduling and guarantee algorithms can possibly give better results for static systems at the price of a longer computation.

A similar real-time scheduling problem is also discussed in 8 where a schedulability formula is given for processes sharing local and remote resources in a multiprocessor environment. The latter paper contains a few ideas that originated this work. Processes have deadlines and the communication is instantaneous. The author applies the rate monotonic analysis 5 to the system, forcing the instances of the processes to be periodic if necessary, and evaluates a series of local and remote blocking that add up in the schedulability formula.
The main contributions of this paper are the following:

end to end deadlines can be expressed as such no arti cial task deadlines. Message and server deadlines do not need to be evaluated; the schedulability analysis is a simple three-step process. Since the rate monotonic analysis is not applied, no period enforcing technique is required, and messages and processes can execute as soon as they are ready. This implies a loss in the schedulability bounds, but makes the implementation a lot easier and the model more understandable; the integrated scheduling of tasks and messages is discussed. Communication is not assumed as instantaneous and neglected, but the scheduling of messages is treated with a good degree of accuracy; the balancing of the timing constraints is obtained as a side product of the schedulability conditions, which in turn are dependent on the computation load imposed on each machine; the schedulability test can be performed at di erent levels of approximation. A less accurate, but faster schedulability test could be used to give run-time guarantees in dynamic systems.

The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 contains a description of the scheduling problem, the process model and our assumptions. Section 3 contains the schedulability analysis that is performed on the client side, Section 4 contains the analysis of the schedulability conditions on the network and in Section 5 the analysis ends by testing the server side. Section 6 contains a discussion on the extensions to the base model and nally, section 7 ends the paper with a short example and the conclusions.

div.head: The Scheduling Problem, Assumptions and Model
div.p: Our scheduling problem assumes a process model. Processes can be client or server type. Both client and server processes can reside on any processor and are statically allocated. Each processor hosts only client or server type processes. We assume an architecture where singleprocessor nodes are connected by a local area network LAN. Each node can contain client processes or server processes together with local processes. It is mandatory that each client requests the same service from the same server all the time. The server creates a di erent task for servicing each request.

Processes are scheduled on processors and messages are scheduled on the network according to xed priority schemes. We assume the priority granularity is su cient to avoid priority i n versions caused by a limited number of available priorities. In reality this is not always feasible when scheduling the network 6 . Processes can be preempted, while messages are transmitted in nonpreemptable units called packets. Both client and server processes can access local shared resources, allocated to tasks for exclusive use and protected by priority ceiling semaphores or by a stack resource policy mechanism. Processes acquire and release them at need, with the restriction that all local resources acquired by a process must be freed before the remote interaction with a server. We assume a simple model where periodic client processes interact with server processes with the following semantics: a client process sends a request to a remote server process, blocking itself while awaiting for the answer. The message containing the request gets scheduled on the network and eventually reaches the server node. On reception of the request, the server process executes and returns a message with the results of its computations. The response message travels the network and is received from the client process which terminates its execution. The priorities to be assigned to processes and messages are not known a-priori but are the result of the schedulability analysis. Later on, we will see how this model can be extended to a collection of nested requests of services.

In all prioritized systems it is normal and desirable that local higher priority tasks steal execution time from lower priority tasks; we will call this time interference time. In the other cases, when a process message has to wait for the execution of a lower priority process or has to wait for a remote service, we h a ve a blocking. Blocking is an undesirable phenomenon, from a local scheduler's point of view, and must be accounted for in the schedulability analysis, usually by adding penalty factors. We call local blocking, the time interval in which a process message is blocked by lower priority local tasks messages executing critical sections because of the network access protocol. Local blocking can be limited i.e. a w orst case bound on the blocking time can be determined by making use of the priority ceiling protocol. The time lost waiting for a remote service is called remote blocking. There is no established technique to deal e ciently with remote blocking.

A solution is presented in 8 where remote critical sections are assigned an higher base priority level plus a level inherited by the client. In that case the remote blocking can be bounded and a ve-term schedulability condition is given. The schedulability formula is rather complex and can easily end up being rather pessimistic. Furthermore, the execution of the remote services remote critical sections is usually done with the priorities inherited by the clients requesting the service; this can easily result in a priority assignment which is far from optimality, as will be shown in section 7.

In the following, the parts of the client processes that are executed before and after the interaction with a server process are called client tasks. Server processes can be called processes or tasks. The following notation is used in the rest of the paper: P i the i-th process M i the i-th message p i priority of the i-th process message N l the number of processes on node l of messages on link l C i the execution time for process P i or the network time needed for the actual transmission of message M i C ij the execution time for the j-th task in process P i B L i local blocking time for process P i message M i B R i remote blocking time for process P i message M i T i period of process P i message M i D i relative deadine of process P i message M i d i absolute deadline of process P i message M i F i global interference on process P i When it is not clear from the context, each symbol will appear with a superscript, c, m or s, indicating it refers to a client process, a message or a server process respectively.

div.head: Scheduling of client tasks
div.p: Each client process gets scheduled according to the following pattern Figure 1: The i-th client process P i consists of two tasks; the rst is executed in the interval I i1 , the second is executed in the interval I i3 . In the middle interval I i2 the request message is sent on the LAN, the server process is executed on the server node and the response message travels back the LAN. The task belonging to I i3 must complete before the deadline of the process. The interval I i2 can be considered a blocking time for the client process and it is in fact a remote blocking, as the process P i is not waiting for the execution of a local computation.
div.formula: client tasks i I I I 1 2 i i 3
div.p: In order to check the schedulability o f P i we need to analyse the joint schedulability of the two tasks that compose it. While the rst task is activated periodically, the second one becomes ready at the beginning of the interval I i3 which is not necessarily periodic. A straightforward rate monotonic analysis is not possible, as it requires additional assumptions or mechanisms necessary to make the activation instants of the tasks periodic. In 8 a technique, called period enforcement, has been proposed in order to force the activation times to be periodic. This technique eases the schedulability analysis and improves the overall processor or network utilization bound 4 . On the other hand, its implementation is not always clear and easy. This is the reason why w e use a di erent kind of analysis: the interference analysis, b y which i t is possible to calculate the maximum possible interference of each process P k in the execution of P i and the latest termination instant for P i . In addition, since each client process su ers not only the interference of higher priority processes but also local B L i and remote B R i blocking, we h a ve t o e v aluate the corresponding factors. For all processes P i the algorithm must check that the computation time C i , plus the interference F i plus the local and remote blocking B L i + B R i , is less than the process deadline D i .

div.head: Scheduling of messages
div.p: In the second step, we shift our attention to the scheduling of the channel. Please consider the periodic client process P i interacting with the server. The channel is used by communication messages in a way m uch similar to the way the processor is used by client processes. In Figure 3 it can be seen that the request message is the rst to travel the network in the time interval I i21 , asking for the server computations. Once the message gets to the server, the server is executed in the interval I i22 and the reply message travels back the network in the opposite direction inside I i23 . The requirement is that the sum of the time intervals I i21 + I i22 + I i23 be less than L i .

The client process, or better, its rst task is activated periodically, but the message ready times are not periodic. Therefore, we c heck the schedulability of messages by c hecking their latest arrival times by means of an interference analysis. Each i n teraction of a client process with a server process implies the delivery of two messages. These messages need to be predictably schedulable on the network the same way client and server processes are scheduled on the CPUs. In the following, by i-th message we mean the network activity jointly needed by the request and response messages; these two messages will be analysed together by the schedulability analysis.
Let's give the following additional de nitions:

M irqst request message produced by the i-th client M i rply reply message received by the i-th client Z i interdiction interval for the i-th message C irqst network time needed for the transmission of the request portion of the i-th message C i rply network time needed for the transmission of the reply portion of the i-th message

If we go back to the client side and see the chain of computations as seen according to the client reference time, then we h a ve the picture represented in Figure 4 where C c i1min is the minimum execution time for the rst client task; t i1 is the start time for the client process, t i2 is the ready time for the request message and d i is the deadline for the response message. From the analysis on the client side we know that the interval reserved to client messages and server computations is an interval large at most L i . In gure this time interval spans between d i and t i2 . Therefore, if d i , t i2 L i than the schedulability test with respect to P c i is veri ed. At this point, we need to be sure that the message M i actually consisting of the two messages M irqst and M i rply travels the network and is received before the relative deadline D m i = d m i , t i2 = L i .

We schedule messages according to the Deadline Monotonic rule: messages are assigned static priorities that are inversely proportional to the relative deadlines di erent from their periods. This explains how the deadline partitioning policy works and why it is e ective: the deadlines of the messages correspond to the maximum allowable remote blocking for the client tasks which is not only function of the client deadlines and computation times, but also of the computation load of the CPU hosting the client process. Please note that at least C c i1 min units of time must elapse from T i1 before the request message M i is ready to be sent, where C c i1 min is the minimum execution time of the rst task of the client process. Furthermore, it is necessary that the answer message gets to the client C i2 units of time before the client deadline, that is d m i t i1 + T i , C c i2 . This means that the client has a time interval, large at least C c i1 min +C c i2 and roughly centered around the beginning of the period of the client process where the request and response messages cannot be sent. This time interval is called the interdiction interval see Figure 5. To c heck the schedulability of the messages we apply the same kind of schedulability analysis that is used for client processes, this time with a change: we shall not consider all the possible interference of the other messages in the client period, but only the interference of the messages that are schedulable outside the interdiction intervals. The schedulability analysis checks whether the messages arrive before their deadlines. Each message M i is delayed by the interference of the other higher priority messages, by the local blocking caused by the need of waiting for lower priority messages and by a remote blocking, corresponding to the execution of the server process. div.p: The interference time from the higher priority messages is not the only time we m ust take i n to account. As for the client tasks, messages are subject to blockings. The priority i n version in this case is not caused by the blocking of messages on critical sections, but by the nonpreemptability of the network transmission units i.e. the packets. Since packets are non-preemptable, it can happen that a high priority message arrives at the network interface right after a lower priority message has started its transmission. Therefore it must wait for the transmission of the lower priority packet before getting into a new contention and be eventually transmitted. This means that the worst case priority inversion suffered by each message is B f , the time necessary to send a message frame. This blocking time is doubled to account for one blocking for the request and another for the response message. Actually, it often happens that the number of priority levels made available by the network protocol does not su ce to map all the message priorities requested by the application. For example, the CAN protocol allows up to 11 bits to express the message identi er encoding the priority but the tokenring protocol allows up to 4 priority bits. By mapping di erent message priorities into the same protocol priority level we h a ve another source of priority i n version. In 6 a w orst case estimate of the penalty factor for the earliest deadline scheduling policy has been given. Most likely a similar bound can be found for the interference analysis, although at this time we simply assume the message priority levels are mapped one-to-one into the available protocol levels. These are the B R i message remote blockings that correspond to the time necessary to the server to make the required computations. div.p: The terms B R i are actually the deadlines imposed on the execution of the server processes, starting from the arrival of the request message from the client. It is easy to see how these values depend from the parameters of the client messages, the channel load and the terms L i which in turn are function of the client process parameters and the load on the client processor.

div.head: Scheduling of server tasks
div.p: The scheduling of the server tasks is analogous to the scheduling of the messages. We use the same kind of schedulability analysis, based on the worst case termination of the server computations, because of the nonperiodicity of the server tasks activation times. The scheduling analysis has the general form 8i = 1 : : :
div.formula: N l C s i + F s i + B Ls i D s i B Rm i 5
div.p: Obviously there is no remote blocking, as the server tasks are activated at the arrival of the request message, possibly su er a local priority i n version when accessing a shared resource, wait the higher priority tasks and then simply execute and terminate.

Server processes are assigned deadlines D s i corresponding to the bounds B Rm i computed in the previous stage. These deadlines are made to correspond to priorities with a deadline monotonic mapping. On the server size we h a ve the same de nitions that we had in the previous sections. Let's see for the last time what are the terms in the formula 5 starting from the interference F i . A not too pessimistic evaluation of the interference of higher priority processes requires the evaluation of the interdiction interval for the server processes. The interdiction interval is the same as for messages, only wider. In fact, the server tasks cannot be executed before end of the rst client task and before the request message gets to the server node. This means that at least C c i1min + C m irqst time units must elapse from the beginning of the client period. Then, the latest execution time for the server task must allow the response message to go beck to the client and the second client task to execute before the end of the period. This means at least C c i2 + C m i rply time units before the end of the client period. Therefore, the interdiction interval is
div.formula: Z s i = C c i1min + C m irqst + C c i2 + C m i rply = C c i1min + C c i2 + C m i .
div.p: The interference from the other local processes P k having higher priority can be evaluated with the same reasoning that is applied to messages in section 4; therefore, the rst approximation of the interference of a process P k on the server process P i is:
div.formula: F i k = C k 1 + D s i , C k + Z s k T k
div.p: and a more accurate formula is
div.formula: F i k = C k 1 + D s i , C k + Z s k T k + min C k ; D s i , C k + Z s k , D s i , C k + Z s k T k T k
div.p: The local blocking is caused by the access to the local shared resources. If these resources are protected by priority ceiling semaphores, then the local blocking of each task is upper bounded by B l the largest local critical section. At this point, since there is no remote blocking, the schedulability of the server tasks can be checked using the following set of formulas. 8i = 1 : : :
div.formula: N l C i + h,1 X k=1 F i + B l D s i B Rm i :
div.p: If the server tasks are schedulable, then we can go back the chain and prove that the messages and the client tasks also are schedulable and terminate the schedulability analysis.

We could think to let the same node manage both client and server processes, although the extension of the algorithm loses some of its desirable properties. Nodes schedule processes in deadline order and the deadline of the server processes is unknown until their clients have been checked. However, the schedulability of the clients can not be checked if the interference from the server processes on the same node is not computed. This would lead to a cycle in the guarantee procedure where the results of each step would not be conclusive until an equilibrium is reached. In principle, the formula could still be used iteratively, but one of the advantages of the algorithm its simplicity would be lost and the procedure would only be a worst case approximation of the one proposed in in 7 except of course for the deadline assignment problem. For the same reason, while it is straightforward to consider the case of nested requests with an arbitrary nesting level all there is to do is repeat the analysis for each level, each time computing the maximum allowed remote blocking and taking it as the deadline for the next server level, this extension requires that the nested levels do not share any s c hedulable resource such as a network link.

div.head: Example and Conclusions
div.p: Before ending the paper we show the usefulness of deriving the timing constraints and the priorities of the messages and the server processes among others from considerations on the processor load, rather than have them blindly inherit the priority or the deadline of the client processes. Later, an hopefully realistic example gives an idea of the procedure to be followed to assign deadline and priorities and to check for the schedulability of a distributed set of interacting client and server processes. div.p: This example shows the procedure that must be followed to assign the priorities and check the schedulability in a relatively complex system consisting of a few nodes connected by a network. div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We present e d a s c heme for scheduling local and remote computations with end-to-end timing constraints. The method takes advantage of a well de ned and restricted programming model where local interactions consist of accesses to shared resources protected by priority ceiling semaphores and the remote interactions are single service requests to a remote server with a blocking semantics. The big advantage of the method proposed in this paper is that it works with end-to-end deadlines. This means that the programmer does not have t o i n vent a deadline partitioning scheme to assign the deadlines and the priorities to the individual tasks and messages. The deadlines and the priorities are automatically and e ciently computed on the basis of the timing requirements of the processes and the processor and network loads.
